questions.text: A team's evaluation dashboard for a customer-facing financial-summary agent reports average end-to-end response latency of 1.8 seconds, well under the team's contractual SLA — which is defined as "95% of requests complete within 3 seconds." Live traffic tracing reveals that 6% of production requests actually exceed 3 seconds, caused by occasional multi-step tool-call retries, yet the eval suite's average-latency figure never flagged this before launch. Which change to the evaluation suite would most directly have caught this SLA compliance gap before it reached production?
questions.explanation: The stem pins the decisive constraint: the SLA is contractually defined at the 95th percentile, and the average-latency metric hid a real 6% violation rate caused by tool-retry tails. Only C changes the evaluation metric definition to match the SLA's own percentile, which would have caught the gap. A (cost) and D (retry timeout) each address a real, adjacent concern — spend and root-cause mitigation — but neither is a metric change that would have surfaced the SLA breach in evaluation. B over-engineers a new service where a metric-reporting change suffices. Answer: C.
questions.topic: evaluation_testing
questions.objective: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)

options.label: A
options.text: Add a cost-per-session metric to track the extra token usage from these retries.
options.explanation: Wrong — this measures spend, which is a real cost-control concern, but it says nothing about whether requests meet the 3-second SLA. It solves an adjacent problem (cost) rather than the latency-compliance gap in the stem.

options.label: B
options.text: Stand up a separate anomaly-detection service that flags sessions with multiple tool retries.
options.explanation: Wrong — this is over-engineered for the ask. Building a new detection service is a bigger lift than simply changing what the existing eval suite reports, and it still doesn't report latency against the SLA directly.

options.label: C
options.text: Report p95 latency alongside the average, matching the SLA's stated percentile.
options.explanation: Correct — the SLA is explicitly defined at the 95th percentile, not the mean. An average can look fine while the tail (driven by retries) breaches the contract; reporting p95 latency directly measures compliance with the stated threshold and would have surfaced the 6% violation rate before launch.

options.label: D
options.text: Raise the internal tool-call retry timeout so fewer requests need a second attempt.
options.explanation: Wrong — this is a plausible production fix for the underlying cause of slow requests, but it changes system behavior, not what the evaluation suite measures. The gap in the stem is a missing metric, not an unfixed retry policy.

questions.text: Production telemetry for a claims-intake assistant shows that 34% of successfully resolved tickets required at least three back-and-forth turns before the customer confirmed the answer was correct. The team's regression suite, however, consists of 500 single-turn prompt/expected-output pairs graded by exact string match against a golden answer. Last week a prompt change raised single-turn accuracy from 91% to 96% and passed the full suite, but complaint volume on multi-turn claims rose 18% in the same week after the change shipped. Which update to the evaluation framework would most effectively catch this class of regression going forward?
questions.explanation: D is correct: the regression escaped because the eval set only contains single-turn exchanges and only checks exact string match, while the real failure mode lives in multi-turn resolution flows and involves judgment calls a string match can't capture. Sampling actual multi-turn transcripts from production and grading them with a mix of a rubric-based LLM judge (for open-ended resolution quality) plus exact-match checks (for required deterministic fields) directly closes both gaps — the missing scenario coverage and the missing grading nuance — which is the mixed-methodology approach the objective asks for. A is wrong because tripling the single-turn set only reduces sampling noise inside the same narrow methodology; it never introduces a multi-turn case, so the identical regression would still pass. B is wrong because it upgrades how existing single-turn pairs are scored but doesn't touch what's being tested — it treats grading strictness as the problem when the root cause is that multi-turn conversations aren't represented in the set at all. C is wrong because routing suspected multi-turn conversations to a human queue is a manual, non-scaling gate applied per release, not a repeatable automated test framework.
questions.topic: Evaluation dataset design — mixed methodologies for multi-turn regression coverage
questions.objective: Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies

options.label: A
options.text: Expand the single-turn regression set from 500 to 1,500 pairs covering more claim types, keeping exact-match grading so the larger sample surfaces edge cases sooner.
options.explanation: Wrong: more volume inside the same single-turn, exact-match methodology reduces sampling noise but never introduces a multi-turn scenario, so the exact regression that just shipped would pass again.

options.label: B
options.text: Replace exact-match grading on the existing single-turn set with a single LLM judge that scores tone, empathy, and clarity on a 1-5 scale for every pair.
options.explanation: Wrong: this improves how the current pairs are scored but doesn't change what's tested — it treats grading strictness as the problem when the actual gap is that multi-turn flows are missing from the set entirely.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a classifier that flags conversations likely to be multi-turn and routes those specific cases to a human review queue before each release.
options.explanation: Wrong: this is a manual, per-release triage gate, not a repeatable automated evaluation framework, and it doesn't scale as conversation volume grows.

options.label: D
options.text: Sample real conversations spanning several exchanges and grade them with a rubric judge plus targeted checks for required fields.
options.explanation: Correct: it closes the representativeness gap by drawing real conversations that go beyond a single exchange and applies a mixed methodology — a rubric judge for subjective resolution quality alongside targeted, deterministic checks for required content.

questions.text: A team improving a customer-support triage agent ran the original system prompt (variant A) for two weeks, then switched 100% of traffic to a revised prompt (variant B) for the next two weeks. QA logs show first-contact-resolution accuracy rose from 81% to 89% (n = 2,300 tickets each period), and the team wants to ship variant B permanently. Before sign-off, a data engineer notices the variant-B period also overlapped with a product update that shifted ticket volume away from billing questions (historically 74% accuracy) toward simpler password-reset requests (historically 93% accuracy). Which action is the most effective next step to determine whether variant B actually improved the agent's performance?
questions.explanation: A wins because it is the only option that addresses the actual flaw: the two periods were sequential, not randomized/concurrent, so the ticket-mix shift (and any other time-correlated factor) is confounded with the prompt change. Randomizing assignment within the same window and stratifying by category isolates the prompt's true effect. B controls for a different variable (time-of-day) than the one flagged, so it solves an adjacent problem. C patches the single known confound via reweighting but leaves the non-randomized, sequential design — and any other lurking time-correlated factor — unaddressed, substituting a proportional correction for a controlled experiment. D substitutes manual review by two people for the metric already computed on 2,300 tickets, which doesn't scale and doesn't touch the confound either.
questions.topic: A/B test validity: confound control via randomization vs. post-hoc fixes
questions.objective: Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements

options.label: A
options.text: Re-run the test as a randomized, concurrent A/B split that routes each incoming ticket to variant A or B independently of category, keep it running for at least one more sprint, and recheck the accuracy gap after stratifying by ticket category.
options.explanation: Correct: randomizing assignment within the same concurrent time window eliminates the ticket-mix confound (and any other unknown time-correlated factor) by construction, and stratifying the analysis by category directly answers whether the lift holds once mix is controlled — this is the only option that fixes the actual experimental design flaw rather than working around one symptom of it.

options.label: B
options.text: Restrict the comparison to tickets that arrived in the same three-hour window (9-11 a.m. weekdays) for both variant A and variant B, so time-of-day traffic patterns no longer explain the accuracy difference between the two prompts.
options.explanation: Wrong: this controls for a time-of-day effect, not the ticket-category mix shift the engineer actually flagged (and the two periods are still non-overlapping calendar weeks, so the underlying sequential-rollout confound remains) — it solves an adjacent problem, not the one observed.

options.label: C
options.text: Reweight each two-week period's ticket mix so billing and password-reset tickets appear in the same 74/26 proportion, then ship variant B if the reweighted accuracy lift is still positive across the 2,300-ticket sample.
options.explanation: Wrong: reweighting only patches the one confound already discovered; it leaves the sequential, non-randomized design in place, so any other factor that moved between the two calendar periods (staffing, ticket difficulty drift, a separate product change) still can't be ruled out — a proportional correction is not a substitute for a controlled comparison.

options.label: D
options.text: Have two senior support leads independently review a random sample of 50 transcripts from each period and rate which variant produced better customer outcomes, then base the ship decision on that combined rating.
options.explanation: Wrong: manual review of 50 transcripts doesn't scale to the 2,300-ticket sample already collected, replaces a measurable metric with subjective judgment, and still says nothing about the ticket-mix confound — it's a human-in-the-loop band-aid, not a fix to the test design.

questions.text: A support-ticket assistant built on Claude answers billing questions using a RAG pipeline over the company's policy wiki. Over the past week, QA flagged 8% of resolved tickets where the assistant confidently cited a refund clause number that does not appear anywhere in the wiki. Engineering pulled the 40 flagged transcripts: in 34 of them, the retriever's top-3 chunks had a cosine similarity below 0.35 to the user's question, well under the pipeline's typical 0.6+ on correctly answered tickets. The system prompt already instructs the model to answer strictly from the retrieved context and to reply "I don't have that information" when the context is insufficient. What should the team investigate first?
questions.explanation: The observed data — low retrieval similarity scores on exactly the flagged tickets, versus healthy scores on correctly answered ones — isolates the root cause to retrieval, not the model or the prompt. B is correct because it follows that evidence to the actual defect. A misdiagnoses it as a model-mismatch problem (symptom not root cause). C treats it as a prompt-compliance problem, an adjacent issue the data doesn't support. D jumps to a new detection subsystem before the simpler, evidence-backed retrieval fix has even been tried (over-engineering).
questions.topic: Diagnosing hallucination root cause in a RAG-backed support assistant
questions.objective: Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)

options.label: A
options.text: The support assistant is running on a smaller model tier than the one used during development testing; upgrading to the larger model in the same family should resolve the fabricated citations.
options.explanation: Wrong diagnosis: the similarity-score data already points to a retrieval failure, not model capability. A larger model given the same irrelevant chunks is just as likely to fill the gap from its parametric memory — this fixes a model-mismatch problem the logs don't actually show.

options.label: B
options.text: The retriever is failing to surface the relevant policy chunks, so the model answers from context lacking the information; the team should investigate why retrieval scores are low for this cluster.
options.explanation: Correct: the data (sub-0.35 similarity vs. the usual 0.6+) points squarely at retrieval, not the model or prompt. When the model is handed context that doesn't contain the answer, it drifts into confident fabrication despite the refusal instruction — so the fix starts by finding why these queries retrieve poorly (embedding mismatch, phrasing, missing content) rather than tuning the model or prompt further.

options.label: C
options.text: The refusal instruction is too easy to override under ambiguous phrasing; adding several few-shot examples of correct 'insufficient context' refusals to the system prompt should stop these fabricated citations from recurring.
options.explanation: Solves an adjacent problem: it assumes the model is ignoring good context, but the transcripts show the context itself was irrelevant. Sharpening the refusal prompt might marginally help but leaves the actual retrieval defect untouched.

options.label: D
options.text: The fabrication rate is high enough to justify building a separate hallucination-detection classifier that scores every response against the retrieved context before it reaches the customer.
options.explanation: Premature complexity: a detection layer treats the symptom (bad outputs reaching users) rather than the diagnosed cause (poor retrieval for this query cluster), and adds a new component before the simpler, already-evident fix has been tried.

questions.text: A customer-support agent built on the Messages API appends the full prior transcript, retrieved KB snippets, and 14 tool definitions to every turn. Production logs show median input tokens climbing from 3,200 at turn 1 to 18,400 by turn 20, p95 latency rising from 4.2s to 13.8s over the same span, and cost per resolved ticket up 3x since launch even though ticket volume is flat. Which change is most likely to reduce cost and latency without degrading resolution quality?
questions.explanation: C is correct: bounding the transcript with a rolling summary caps the token growth that's driving both the cost and latency trends, and layering prompt caching on the now-stable prefix captures the rest of the available savings. A only addresses per-token price, not the growing context or the latency it causes, and risks quality loss on long tickets. B caches the wrong part of the prompt — the stable prefix isn't what's growing, so cost and latency keep climbing with the transcript. D targets timeouts/retries, a different problem than the cost and latency trend described in the logs.
questions.topic: Managing multi-turn context growth: summarization + prompt caching for cost/latency
questions.objective: Optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs

options.label: A
options.text: Switch the underlying model to a smaller, cheaper variant for every turn, keeping the existing full-transcript prompt structure unchanged.
options.explanation: Cuts per-token price but leaves the root cause untouched: the transcript still grows unbounded, so latency keeps climbing with turn count and a weaker model is more likely to lose track of earlier ticket details, trading cost for quality on long conversations.

options.label: B
options.text: Enable prompt caching on the system prompt and the 14 tool definitions, leaving the growing conversation transcript uncached and appended in full each turn.
options.explanation: A reasonable first move that trims cost on the stable portion of the prompt, but the transcript is the part that's actually growing turn over turn; caching only the fixed prefix does nothing to cap the 18,400-token payload or the latency that scales with it.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace turns older than the last 4 exchanges with a rolling summary, and cache the now-stable system prompt and tool-definition prefix ahead of it.
options.explanation: Bounds the transcript so input size stops growing with conversation length, directly attacking both the token trend and the latency trend, while caching the now-fixed prefix captures the remaining savings on the parts of the prompt that don't change turn to turn.

options.label: D
options.text: Raise the max_tokens output limit and add exponential-backoff retries around calls that time out under the current transcript size.
options.explanation: Addresses a reliability symptom (timeouts) rather than the cost and latency problem the logs describe; a larger output budget and more retries would, if anything, increase average cost and tail latency on an already-oversized context.

questions.text: Your team operates a customer-support agent built on the Claude API that processes roughly 40,000 conversations a day through three stages: document retrieval, tool execution, and the model call itself. Over the past week, the dashboard's overall p95 latency climbed from 3.2 seconds to 9.8 seconds. The team's current dashboard only reports total request count and overall error rate, so support engineers can confirm conversations are slower but cannot tell which of the three stages is driving the regression. Which approach would most effectively let the team identify, and continue tracking, which stage is responsible for latency regressions like this one?
questions.explanation: D is correct: tagging each stage (retrieval, tool execution, model call) with OpenTelemetry spans under a shared trace ID gives a per-stage, per-conversation latency breakdown that isolates the culprit today and keeps working for future regressions. A is a plausible first instinct but only confirms the regression exists end-to-end — a canary with a single pass/fail threshold on total latency solves the "did it get slower" question, not the "where" question the team already answered by reproducing the slowdown. B substitutes a brittle text-search heuristic (grepping verbose logs for "slow") for a structured, queryable signal; it depends on someone guessing the right keyword and re-reading logs by hand after every incident rather than exposing stage boundaries directly. C is a manual, human-in-the-loop workaround that can diagnose one incident but doesn't scale to 40,000 conversations a day or persist as a monitoring capability once the on-call engineer moves on.
questions.topic: Distributed tracing for multi-stage latency regressions
questions.objective: Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools

options.label: A
options.text: Deploy a synthetic canary transaction every 5 minutes that runs the entire pipeline end-to-end and page on-call if total round-trip latency exceeds 5 seconds.
options.explanation: Wrong: this detects that a regression is happening but gives no stage-level breakdown, so the team is back to square one on locating the cause — it solves the adjacent problem of alerting, not diagnosis.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise every service's log level to DEBUG and have engineers grep the merged log stream for slow requests during the next reported incident.
options.explanation: Wrong: this is a brittle text-search heuristic over unstructured logs, dependent on guessing the right search terms, instead of using the actual observability mechanism (structured, correlated spans) built for exactly this.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask on-call engineers to manually time each pipeline stage with print statements inserted at the start and end of every stage the next few times a slow conversation is reported.
options.explanation: Wrong: a manual, human-in-the-loop timing exercise doesn't scale to 40,000 conversations a day and produces no durable dashboard for future regressions.

options.label: D
options.text: Instrument the retrieval, tool-execution, and model-call stages with OpenTelemetry spans sharing one trace ID, then chart p95 latency per stage.
options.explanation: Correct: shared-trace-ID spans per stage give an automatic, ongoing, per-stage latency breakdown that pinpoints the current regression and surfaces future ones without manual effort.

questions.text: A financial-services support bot has been in production for six weeks. Before every release, the eval harness reports exactly two numbers: exact-match accuracy against a 500-item gold set (currently 91%) and p95 latency (currently 1.1s). Last week's incident review found that in 4% of sampled transcripts, an unmasked account number appeared inside a tool-call argument that got written to a third-party logging service — even though the final chat reply shown to the customer was clean in every case. Which single metric should the team add to the release gate to catch this class of incident before the next deployment?
questions.explanation: A is correct: the leak occurred in tool-call arguments written to logs, not in the final reply, so the gate must score PII exposure across the full trace (tool calls, arguments, intermediate steps) to catch it — accuracy and latency say nothing about this failure mode. B raises the accuracy bar, but accuracy against a gold-answer set measures correctness of the final response, not what leaks through intermediate tool traffic; a bot could hit 97% accuracy and still leak account numbers in tool calls. C scans the same surface that was already proven clean in the incident — the customer-facing message — so it would pass every future release while the actual leak channel (logged tool-call arguments) goes unchecked. D reaches for a bespoke ML classifier and a new microservice before establishing the simpler fix: extending the existing redaction/detection check to cover the full trace; standing up new infrastructure is premature complexity for a scope problem.
questions.topic: Evaluation & Testing – defining safety/security metrics alongside accuracy and latency
questions.objective: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)

options.label: A
options.text: Score PII-leakage rate across full tool-call traces, not just the final reply
options.explanation: Correct: the incident happened inside tool-call arguments sent to logging, a surface neither accuracy nor latency touches. Auditing the full trace for unmasked identifiers directly targets where the leak occurs and can be gated per release.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise the required exact-match accuracy threshold from 91% to 97% before release
options.explanation: Wrong surface: exact-match accuracy grades whether the final answer content is correct, not whether sensitive data leaked into logs via tool arguments. A model can be highly accurate and still leak PII outside the graded response.

options.label: C
options.text: Scan only the final customer-facing message for unmasked account numbers before send
options.explanation: Solves an adjacent problem: the incident review already confirmed the final reply was clean every time — the leak was in the logged tool-call arguments. This check would pass release after release while the real channel stays unmonitored.

options.label: D
options.text: Train a dedicated PII-classification model and stand up a new scoring microservice for it
options.explanation: Over-engineered first step: before building custom ML infrastructure, the team hasn't even extended its existing detection logic to cover tool-call traces. A scope fix to the current check is the minimal effective change; a new service is premature.

questions.text: The eval team for an enterprise contract-review assistant maintains a 240-item regression suite that grades every response with a single LLM-judge prompt on a 1-5 rubric. A Q3 production review found that in 18% of contract clauses containing a numeric penalty term (e.g., "2% per day late fee"), the judge scored the response a 4 or 5 even though the assistant cited the wrong percentage or day count. The team must redesign the dataset and grading pipeline so this class of error is caught before the next release. Which TWO changes would most strongly improve detection of this failure mode?
questions.explanation: C and D are correct. C adds a deterministic, code-based grader for the exact field the LLM judge keeps missing, turning the framework into a genuine mixed-methodology pipeline (programmatic check + model-graded rubric), each doing what it's suited for. D fixes the dataset side of the same gap: the 240-item suite under-represents the specific clause type where failures cluster, so a stratified sample of real production cases closes that coverage hole. A only strengthens the same probabilistic judge that already missed the pattern (prompt-when-you-need-a-guarantee). B improves inter-judge agreement but two LLM judges can share the identical blind spot for extracting a number from prose, so it doesn't add a verification mechanism. E is a manual band-aid that doesn't scale and doesn't improve the automated eval framework itself.
questions.topic: Mixed-methodology eval design: pairing deterministic graders with LLM judges and targeted dataset expansion
questions.objective: Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies

options.label: A
options.text: Add three more few-shot examples of numeric-accuracy failures to the LLM-judge prompt, sharpening how it penalizes a wrong figure.
options.explanation: Still routes the fix through the same probabilistic judge that already missed 18% of these cases; better prompting reduces but cannot guarantee catching an exact numeric mismatch, so nearby values will keep slipping through.

options.label: B
options.text: Run every clause through two independent LLM judges and route any pair whose scores differ by more than one point to manual reconciliation.
options.explanation: Improves consistency between judges but both are drawing on the same kind of pattern-matching over prose; they can agree while both missing the same wrong number, since neither is verifying the figure against a ground-truth source.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a deterministic grader that extracts the cited percentage and day count and compares them against the source clause's values, failing the item on any mismatch.
options.explanation: Pairs a code-based, exact-match check for the verifiable numeric field with the existing model-graded rubric for tone and completeness -- a mixed-methodology framework where each grader handles what it is actually reliable at.

options.label: D
options.text: Expand the dataset with a stratified sample of production clauses carrying numeric penalty terms, drawn from the contract types where the 18% miss rate appeared.
options.explanation: Targets the actual dataset gap: the existing 240-item random draw under-represents the exact clause type where failures cluster, so adding representative real cases closes the coverage hole the 18% figure exposed.

options.label: E
options.text: Route every response that contains a numeric penalty term to a human reviewer queue before it is allowed into production release.
options.explanation: A manual review band-aid that catches individual cases but doesn't scale with contract volume and leaves the automated eval framework itself unable to detect this failure class going forward.

questions.text: A team runs a one-week, 50/50 experiment comparing two system-prompt variants for a billing-support Claude agent. Across 240 resolved conversations, Variant B shows a 6-point higher first-contact resolution rate than Variant A, but the difference carries a p-value of 0.12. Support leadership wants a rollout decision before the next planning cycle. Which TWO actions are most likely to produce a defensible decision?
questions.explanation: Keys are C and E. C is correct because the observed 6-point lift is not yet statistically significant (p=0.12) at n=240, and the direct fix is running the test to the sample size a proper power calculation demands rather than guessing. E is correct because holding resolution rate as the single pre-registered metric prevents the multiple-comparisons problem of hunting through new metrics for a significant result. A is a distractor because shipping on a non-significant lift confuses a plausible trend with a confirmed effect. B is a distractor because post-hoc subgroup fishing on an already-small sample is a classic way to manufacture a spurious significant result. D is a distractor because manual transcript review is a human-in-the-loop band-aid that doesn't scale and ignores the metric the experiment was built to answer.
questions.topic: A/B testing statistical rigor and iteration
questions.objective: Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements

options.label: A
options.text: Ship Variant B to all traffic now and rely on post-launch dashboards to catch any regressions.
options.explanation: Wrong: a p=0.12 lift hasn't cleared significance, so treating it as a confirmed win means any post-launch wobble is indistinguishable from the noise the test was supposed to rule out.

options.label: B
options.text: Segment the 240 conversations by customer tier and roll out only to the subgroup where the lift is significant.
options.explanation: Wrong: slicing an already-small sample into subgroups and picking whichever one clears significance is data dredging — with enough slices, some subgroup will look significant by chance.

options.label: C
options.text: Extend the test until the sample size meets the pre-test power calculation for this metric.
options.explanation: Correct: the test is underpowered for the observed effect size; running it to the sample size a power calculation requires is the direct way to find out if the 6-point lift is real.

options.label: D
options.text: Have two senior engineers read a transcript sample from each variant and vote on which reads better.
options.explanation: Wrong: a manual read-through by two reviewers substitutes subjective preference for the resolution-rate metric the experiment exists to measure, and it doesn't scale to future tests.

options.label: E
options.text: Keep the success measure as the sole pre-registered metric and avoid adding new metrics mid-test.
options.explanation: Correct: locking to the one metric the test was designed around prevents the false-positive inflation that comes from testing many metrics until one happens to clear significance.

questions.text:
A platform team reviews five flagged sessions from an internal HR-policy assistant that retrieves passages from a document store and drafts an answer for employees. For each session below, classify the root cause using this shared taxonomy:

- **Prompt failure** — the instructions given to the model don't address this input's shape, and supplying the missing guidance fixes the behavior with the same model and the same retrieved passages.
- **Model capability mismatch** — the task is genuinely beyond what the model can reliably do here, and it still fails even after adding explicit step-by-step guidance and breaking the task into smaller pieces.
- **Hallucination** — the model states a specific detail that cannot be found anywhere in the material it was given, even though that material was confirmed correct and complete.
- **Data/retrieval gap** — the model never had access to the right source content in the first place, no matter how the instructions are worded.

Session 1: An employee asks what the current parental-leave policy allows. The assistant's answer quotes eligibility rules and page numbers that, on inspection, match the 2019 employee handbook word for word. Engineering confirms the 2026 handbook revision containing the current parental-leave section was never indexed into the assistant's document store, so that content simply isn't available to be retrieved. The answer is an accurate, faithful summary of the document the model actually received.

Session 2: An employee asks about the tuition-reimbursement cap. The assistant answers, "$5,000 per year, and you get a 90-day grace period to submit late receipts." The retrieved passage — confirmed to be the current, correct policy text, a single short sentence — states only the $5,000 cap and nothing else; a full-text search of every document in the knowledge base turns up no mention of any grace period anywhere. The instructions already tell the model, in plain terms, to state only what the retrieved passage says and add nothing beyond it, with a worked example showing exactly that behavior, and the model correctly reproduces every other detail in the passage exactly.

Session 3: An employee writes: "Can I stack bereavement leave with my PTO the same week, and does my manager sign off on both separately?" The instructions the model works from walk through answering one policy topic per message and say nothing about a message naming two topics at once. Both the bereavement passage and the PTO approval-chain passage were successfully retrieved and sat in the model's context. The assistant answers only the PTO half and drops the bereavement question entirely. When an analyst added one line to the instructions — "if a message names more than one policy area, answer each one in turn" — and reran the identical message with the identical retrieved passages, the assistant answered both halves correctly.

Session 4: An employee asks how many PTO days they'll have banked by a given date, under a schedule with a lower accrual rate before three years of tenure, a higher rate after, mid-year-hire proration, and a five-day carryover cap. The instructions already spell out the arithmetic step by step and include a fully worked example using the same tiered, prorated structure. The assistant's total is still wrong — it double-counts the carryover. An analyst reruns the request broken into three separate prompts, one per component (base accrual, proration, carryover), then manually adds the three model outputs together; the final sum is still incorrect because one of the three component outputs is itself wrong.

Session 5: A US-based employee asks about the remote-work stipend. The assistant states a dollar threshold that engineering confirms belongs to the UK office's remote-work policy, not the US one. The document store has no field tagging which country or region each policy document applies to, so the retriever has no way to prefer the US document over the UK one for this employee — a mismatch that exists before any instruction ever reaches the model. The returned answer matches the UK document's numbers exactly.
questions.explanation:
Row 1 (Session 1) → Data/retrieval gap: the answer matches the retrieved document verbatim (faithful, not fabricated), and engineering confirms the correct 2026 content was never indexed — no instruction could fix content that isn't in the index, and there's no invented detail to call hallucination.

Row 2 (Session 2) → Hallucination: the retrieved passage is confirmed current and complete, the model correctly reproduces everything else in it, and an explicit "state only what's in the passage" instruction with a worked example is already present — so it isn't a retrieval gap, isn't a prompt gap, and getting one short sentence right except for one invented clause isn't a capability ceiling; it's a fabricated detail with zero support anywhere in the knowledge base.

Row 3 (Session 3) → Prompt failure: both correct passages were already in context (rules out retrieval gap), and adding a single line of guidance — with the same model and same passages — immediately fixed the behavior, which is the direct empirical test that rules out model capability mismatch (a real ceiling wouldn't dissolve from one instruction line) and rules out hallucination (nothing was fabricated, a sub-question was simply dropped).

Row 4 (Session 4) → Model capability mismatch: the instructions already include explicit step-by-step arithmetic and a matching worked example (rules out prompt failure), and decomposing the task into isolated sub-prompts with the final addition done by a human still produces a wrong component (rules out both prompt failure and any recombination/instruction issue) — the failure survives every standard prompting fix, which is the signature of a genuine reasoning ceiling rather than a fixable instruction gap.

Row 5 (Session 5) → Data/retrieval gap: the document store has no region field at all, so the wrong-country document is structurally unavoidable regardless of what the model is told to do — this is a second, distinct instance of the same category as Session 1 (missing/wrong source content upstream of the model), confirming the option is meant to key more than one row rather than being a one-off.
questions.topic: evaluation_testing
questions.objective: Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)

rows.text: Session 1: parental-leave answer matches the 2019 handbook verbatim; the 2026 revision was never indexed into the document store.

Session 2: assistant adds a 90-day grace period found nowhere in the confirmed-correct, complete retrieved passage or the rest of the knowledge base, despite an explicit anti-embellishment instruction already in place.
Session 3: assistant drops the bereavement half of a two-part question even though both passages were retrieved; adding one line of instruction fixed it with the same model and same passages.
Session 4: tiered/prorated PTO accrual math is still wrong despite explicit step-by-step instructions, a worked example, and decomposition into isolated sub-prompts with manual recombination.
Session 5: remote-work stipend answer matches the UK policy instead of the US one because the document store has no region tagging at all, independent of any instruction to the model.

questions.text: A fintech company's Claude-based customer support agent has a system prompt stating that refund offers must never exceed the $500 policy cap. Production logs from the past two weeks show that in 8% of transcripts, the agent quoted a refund figure above $500 anyway, almost entirely on turns where the customer described an unusually sympathetic circumstance (a medical emergency, a bereavement, a shipping disaster). The support director wants a fix before the next release. Which action would most effectively prevent this from recurring?
questions.explanation: B is correct: an 8% breach rate under an explicit system-prompt cap shows the model can be swayed by emotionally compelling context, so the fix must not depend on the model's compliance at all. A programmatic check that parses the proposed refund figure out of the response and blocks anything over $500 before it reaches the customer enforces the cap deterministically, closing exactly the gap the logs revealed. A is tempting because prompting is the usual lever, but it only makes non-compliance less likely, not impossible — the same 8%-style failure will resurface under a new sympathetic scenario. C sounds thorough but is a manual band-aid layered on premature complexity: building and training a separate classifier plus a human review queue is slower to ship and still lets the non-compliant offer reach the transcript before anyone catches it. D improves visibility into how often violations happen but is a detection change, not a prevention change — it solves the adjacent problem of measurement, not the refund cap itself.
questions.topic: Deterministic guardrails vs. prompting for policy enforcement
questions.objective: Implement guardrails and safety controls

options.label: A
options.text: Revise the system prompt with firmer wording and few-shot examples showing refunds capped at $500.
options.explanation: Strengthening the prompt reduces the odds of a violation but still relies on probabilistic compliance — the same emotionally-charged scenario pattern that caused the current 8% breach rate can defeat a firmer prompt too.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a code check that parses the reply's dollar figure and blocks delivery if it clears the cap.
options.explanation: Correct: a programmatic, deterministic check that inspects the reply's dollar figure enforces the cap independent of what the model decides to say, closing the gap the logs exposed.

options.label: C
options.text: Train a compliance classifier to flag transcripts with refunds over $500 and route them for human approval.
options.explanation: Building and training a separate model plus a review queue is premature complexity for this problem, and routing to a human after the fact doesn't stop the non-compliant offer from being generated and shown first.

options.label: D
options.text: Increase weekly transcript sampling from 5% to 20% to catch $500-cap violations sooner overall.
options.explanation: More sampling improves detection and reporting of violations but does nothing to stop them from occurring — it addresses visibility, not the underlying enforcement gap.

questions.text: A due-diligence team at an asset management firm uses Claude to condense 200-page S-1 filings into one-page risk memos for analysts. During a Q3 internal audit, compliance sampled 50 memos and found that in 6 of them, the memo cited a precise, specific-looking figure (for example, "total addressable market of $4.2B") that does not appear anywhere in the corresponding source filing. Engineering re-ran the retrieval logs for all 6 cases and confirmed that the correct, current-version filing chunks were passed to the model each time. Which of the following best characterizes the risk this observation reveals?
questions.explanation: The retrieval logs confirm the correct current-version chunks reached the model in all 6 cases, which rules out A (stale cache) directly. B is undercut because the cited figures are described as internally consistent with each memo's own surrounding narrative — i.e., different values per filing — which a reused few-shot placeholder would not produce. D reframes the finding as a flaw in the audit's manual spot-check methodology rather than engaging with the fact retrieval correctness was already verified programmatically, so it sidesteps the evidence instead of explaining it. C is correct: the model is generating precise, fluent, narratively coherent numeric detail that has no basis in the retrieved source text — confabulation, a known LLM failure mode where output fluency and internal consistency are not signals of factual grounding, and one that persists even when the retrieval pipeline itself is working correctly.
questions.topic: Confabulation and grounding failures in retrieval-augmented LLM outputs
questions.objective: Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems

options.label: A
options.text: The retrieval pipeline is serving cached chunks from a prior version of the S-1 filing, so the model is citing figures that were accurate for an earlier draft but not the current one.
options.explanation: Ruled out by the evidence itself: engineering re-ran the retrieval logs and confirmed the correct current-version chunks were passed in all 6 cases, so a stale-cache explanation is directly contradicted rather than merely unlikely.

options.label: B
options.text: The few-shot examples embedded in the prompt template contain sample dollar figures that the model is pattern-matching and reproducing across unrelated filings.
options.explanation: A real prompt-engineering failure mode, but it predicts the same placeholder figures recurring verbatim across memos; here the fabricated numbers are described as consistent with each memo's own distinct narrative, which a copied template artifact would not produce.

options.label: C
options.text: The model is confabulating precise, narratively consistent numeric details that have no grounding in the retrieved source text, a known limitation where fluency does not indicate factual accuracy.
options.explanation: Matches the evidence exactly: retrieval was verified correct, yet the model still produced fabricated but internally coherent figures. This is the documented confabulation failure mode, which occurs independently of whether the pipeline supplied the right context.

options.label: D
options.text: The compliance team's manual page-by-page spot-check against the source PDF introduces its own transcription error at a comparable 6-in-50 rate, so the flagged figures may not be genuine model errors.
options.explanation: A human-review band-aid argument that questions the auditors rather than the system, and it does not account for the fact that retrieval correctness was confirmed through logs, not manual comparison, leaving the fabricated-figure pattern unexplained.

questions.text: Production logs for an autonomous refund-processing agent show it correctly handled 340 of 352 refund requests this week without any issue. However, 3 of the 12 refunds it approved above $2,000 were later found to violate a discount-stacking exception the agent had misapplied, costing the company several thousand dollars in unrecoverable payouts. The team wants a control that closes this specific failure mode without adding an approval step to the 96% of requests the agent already handles correctly. Which approach is most effective for this workflow?
questions.explanation: D is correct: it puts a deterministic, enforced checkpoint at the tool boundary itself, scoped to exactly the risk tier where the failures occurred (refunds above $2,000), while leaving the already-reliable low-value path untouched. A is wrong because routing all 352 requests through one queue erases the throughput benefit of automation for the 96% that were never the problem, and doesn't target the specific high-value policy-exception failure. B is wrong because clearer prompt wording only reduces the odds of the agent misreading the policy again — it's a probabilistic fix layered onto a control gap, and the after-the-fact weekly log doesn't stop the money from leaving before anyone reviews it. C is wrong because it depends on the model reliably emitting a specific text tag and an external script correctly catching it; any drift in phrasing or a skipped tag lets a bad refund straight through, whereas D enforces the check as a structural property of the tool call rather than a convention the model has to remember to follow.
questions.topic: Risk-tiered human-in-the-loop approval gates
questions.objective: Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies

options.label: A
options.text: Require every refund request, at any dollar amount, to pass through a shared human approval queue before execution.
options.explanation: Wrong: this eliminates the throughput benefit of automation for the 96% of requests that were already handled correctly, and it doesn't specifically target the high-value policy-exception failure that actually occurred — it's a blanket manual gate standing in for a scoped architectural fix.

options.label: B
options.text: Strengthen the system prompt's refund-policy wording with clearer discount-stacking examples, and review a weekly log of the agent's refund decisions.
options.explanation: Wrong: clearer prompt wording lowers the chance of a repeat misread but gives no guarantee, and reviewing a weekly log is after-the-fact — it doesn't stop a misapplied high-value refund from executing in the first place.

options.label: C
options.text: Have the agent tag its response text with NEEDS_REVIEW for exception refunds above $2,000, and have a downstream script grep for that tag before releasing funds.
options.explanation: Wrong: this is a brittle text-parsing heuristic bolted on after generation — if the model phrases its output differently or omits the tag on an edge case, the refund releases with no check at all, unlike an enforced structural gate.

options.label: D
options.text: Configure the refund tool so any payout above $2,000 is blocked from completing until a human signs off, while lower payouts finish automatically.
options.explanation: Correct: this builds the checkpoint into the tool call itself, scoped precisely to the risk tier where the actual failures happened, so high-value exceptions get a mandatory human decision while the reliable low-value majority keeps executing automatically.

questions.text: During a HIPAA compliance audit of a hospital's Claude-based clinical documentation assistant, the security team finds that troubleshooting logs containing full API prompts, including patient names and medical record numbers, have been retained for 90 days by a third-party observability vendor that has never signed a Business Associate Agreement. What is the most effective first step to close this compliance gap before the assistant returns to production use?
questions.explanation: A is correct: it closes the gap at the point of actual exposure with a deterministic, code-level control (strip PHI from prompts before they leave the trust boundary) and formalizes the legal requirement (BAA) for whatever residual data remains — matching both the technical and contractual halves of the HIPAA violation. B is a plausible-sounding fix but is premature over-engineering: standing up an entirely new in-house logging platform with its own encryption, RBAC, and audit trail takes months and doesn't address the immediate fact that unredacted PHI is currently leaving the boundary today. C relies on the model reliably choosing never to emit PHI in its own output — a probabilistic instruction where the residual failure rate is exactly the kind of risk a deterministic redaction filter is meant to eliminate. D is a manual human-in-the-loop band-aid: reviewing log files by hand doesn't scale past a handful of requests and leaves the vendor relationship itself out of compliance in the interim.
questions.topic: HIPAA compliance - PHI in third-party logging pipelines
questions.objective: Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)

options.label: A
options.text: Add a redaction step to the logging pipeline that strips patient names and MRNs from prompts before they leave the trust boundary, and sign a BAA with the vendor for any residual PHI that remains.
options.explanation: Correct: fixes the technical exposure with a deterministic pipeline control and satisfies the HIPAA contractual requirement for whatever PHI still reaches the vendor, addressing both dimensions of the audit finding.

options.label: B
options.text: Replace the vendor with a newly built in-house logging platform that encrypts prompts at rest, enforces role-based access controls, and produces its own compliance audit trail for every request sent.
options.explanation: Wrong: a sensible long-term architecture, but building a whole new logging platform is premature complexity for a gap that a redaction filter plus a BAA closes immediately; it leaves PHI exposed for the months the migration takes.

options.label: C
options.text: Update the assistant's system prompt to instruct it to never include patient names or medical record numbers in any output that might later be logged for troubleshooting purposes.
options.explanation: Wrong: relies on probabilistic prompt compliance to prevent PHI from ever appearing, where what's needed is a deterministic guarantee the logging pipeline itself enforces, not a request the model can occasionally miss.

options.label: D
options.text: Have the compliance officer manually review and redact each troubleshooting log file by hand before it is forwarded to the observability vendor for analysis.
options.explanation: Wrong: a manual, human-in-the-loop review doesn't scale with log volume and does nothing to resolve the underlying absence of a BAA with the vendor.

questions.text: A regional bank's loan pre-screening assistant is built on a fine-tuned Claude deployment that returns an approve/hold/decline recommendation plus a short rationale for each applicant. A quarterly fairness audit stratified 4,000 recent cases by applicant zip code and found the hold/decline rate diverged by more than 9 percentage points across zip codes — even though zip code is never passed to the model as an input field. The assistant is currently on a risk-review hold pending a fix. Which action is most likely to actually close this gap before the assistant is cleared to resume production traffic?
questions.explanation: B is correct: the audit shows a proxy-variable problem — some field the model does see (employer name, school, address history) is standing in for zip code — so the fix has to (1) find the proxy deterministically via a correlation analysis, (2) put a hard, non-probabilistic control in front of any recommendation that touches a flagged field (a documented human-review queue), and (3) keep a standing, auditable transparency artifact (per-cohort deltas on the risk dashboard) so recurrence is caught automatically rather than at the next quarterly audit. A fails because it asks the model to self-police a correlation via instructions and trusts its own stated rationale as proof of compliance — a probabilistic fix for what the audit shows is a systematic, code-level leakage problem. C treats the symptom instead of the mechanism: dropping two named fields might reduce this particular disparity, but nothing in the change verifies that was the actual source or would catch the next proxy that emerges after retraining, and it adds no ongoing monitoring or documentation trail. D is a manual band-aid: a 10% weekly manual sample doesn't scale to full production volume, catches disparities only after applicants are affected, and isn't scoped to the geographic signal the audit actually flagged.
questions.topic: Remediating a proxy-variable bias finding in a lending assistant
questions.objective: Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)

options.label: A
options.text: Revise the assistant's system prompt to instruct it to disregard any correlation with geography or demographic group when generating an approval recommendation, and have it note its compliance in the rationale it returns.
options.explanation: Wrong: this relies on the model reliably following an instruction not to use a signal it was never explicitly given in the first place — it doesn't identify or block the actual proxy field causing the leakage, so the disparity can persist while the returned rationale merely claims compliance.

options.label: B
options.text: Run a proxy-variable analysis on the input fields (employer name, education institution, address history) to find which ones correlate with zip code, route flagged recommendations to a documented human-review queue, and log per-cohort approval deltas on the risk dashboard.
options.explanation: Correct: this locates the actual proxy driving the disparity, adds a deterministic gate (human review) rather than a prompt-level ask, and creates a standing, auditable transparency mechanism that catches drift going forward — matching what the audit finding actually requires.

options.label: C
options.text: Retrain the pre-screening classifier on a feature set that drops employer name and education institution, then redeploy immediately, since removing those two fields should eliminate the geographic disparity the audit measured.
options.explanation: Wrong: this guesses at the proxy fields without confirming them against the audit data, skips any verification that the disparity actually closes, and leaves no ongoing monitoring or documentation — a plausible move that fixes only the symptom the audit happened to catch.

options.label: D
options.text: Direct the compliance team to manually re-check a random 10% sample of the assistant's approval recommendations each week and escalate any that appear inconsistent with an applicant's stated income and credit profile.
options.explanation: Wrong: a 10% manual sample doesn't scale to the assistant's full production volume, only surfaces problems after applicants have already been affected, and isn't even targeted at the geographic proxy signal the audit flagged.

questions.text: A fintech company's Claude-based support agent has access to a `transfer_funds` tool. The system prompt states a $5,000 daily transfer limit per customer and instructs the agent to refuse any transfer that would exceed it. Production logs from the past week show that 4% of executed transfers exceeded that stated limit anyway, and finance flagged the discrepancy during weekly reconciliation. The team needs the most effective fix to eliminate this class of incident before the next release. Which approach should they take?
questions.explanation: C is correct: it moves the $5,000 cap out of the probabilistic prompt layer and into a deterministic, code-level precondition inside the transfer_funds handler itself, so every request is checked against the account's stored limit before execution regardless of how the agent reasoned about the instruction. A reinforces the exact mechanism that already produced the 4% failure rate — a stronger prompt is still a probabilistic ask, not a guarantee. B adds a real, sensible-sounding control (anomaly scoring plus human review) but it's still probabilistic detection layered with a manual review bottleneck that won't scale with transaction volume, rather than a hard precondition that closes the gap for every request. D fixes an adjacent problem: routing larger transfers to a better-instructed agent only raises the same unenforced, prompt-based compliance risk to a different dollar threshold and leaves everything below it unchecked.
questions.topic: Guardrails: deterministic tool-level validation vs. prompt reinforcement
questions.objective: Implement guardrails and safety controls

options.label: A
options.text: Revise the system prompt to restate the $5,000 daily transfer limit more emphatically and add three few-shot examples showing the agent correctly refusing an over-limit request.
options.explanation: This reinforces the same probabilistic instruction that already produced the 4% failure rate; a more emphatic prompt still relies on the model choosing to comply on every single request, which is exactly what failed in production.

options.label: B
options.text: Introduce an anomaly-detection model trained on six months of transaction history that scores each transfer request and flags likely policy violations for a human analyst to review beforehand.
options.explanation: A plausible-looking control, but it substitutes a probabilistic scoring model plus a manual review step for a simple fixed-threshold check, adding latency and an analyst bottleneck that won't keep pace with transfer volume and still won't catch every over-limit case.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a server-side check in the transfer_funds handler that compares the requested amount to the account's stored daily limit and returns an error instead of executing when it is exceeded.
options.explanation: This is a deterministic, code-level precondition that runs on every call to the tool, so an over-limit transfer is rejected outright before execution rather than depending on the agent choosing to enforce the policy correctly.

options.label: D
options.text: Route any transfer request above $1,000 to a separate agent instance configured with more detailed compliance instructions and escalation guidance.
options.explanation: This solves a different problem — routing high-value transfers to a more heavily instructed agent — while leaving the underlying enforcement still prompt-based and unchecked for transfers below the routing threshold.

questions.text:
A regional hospital network deployed an LLM-based clinical-documentation assistant that transcribes doctor-patient visit recordings and drafts the structured after-visit summary — diagnosis, medications with dosages, and follow-up instructions — which a nurse then reviews, edits if needed, and signs into the EHR. The vendor contract sets a hard requirement: medication-dosage errors in signed summaries must stay below 1 per 500 visits, since a wrong dosage is the single patient-safety risk the hospital's monthly QA rubric exists to catch.

In July's audit of 500 signed summaries, the QA team found two distinct patterns:

1. In 22 summaries, the drafted dosage (e.g., "400 mg" when the transcript said "40 mg" or mentioned no dose at all) did not appear anywhere in the visit recording or the patient's prior chart, and did not match any current or previously superseded formulary value for that drug — the number was invented outright, and regenerating the summary from the same recording reproduced the same invented dose each time. QA reviewed both the recordings and the prior chart entries for embedded or adversarial phrasing and found no such signature in either source.

2. In another 15 summaries, the drafted dosage matched the recording exactly, but a post-audit survey of the signing nurses found they had stopped cross-checking AI drafts word-for-word against the recording because, in their experience, the summaries "always read fluently and confidently" and had never contained an error they personally caught before.

Which TWO of the following are the failure modes most clearly evidenced by this audit?
questions.explanation: The audit reveals two independent, well-documented LLM system risks. Finding #1 (22 cases) is confabulation (D): a fabricated dosage grounded in nothing -- not the transcript, not the chart, not any current or past formulary value -- and reproducible, which fluent phrasing renders invisible on a quick read. Options A (prompt injection) and C (training-data drift) are ruled out by explicit details in the stem: QA checked both the recordings and the chart for adversarial phrasing and found none, and the invented numbers matched no real formulary value ever published, foreclosing the "stale-but-genuine" drift theory. Finding #2 (15 cases) is automation bias (E): reviewers' own admissions that fluent, consistently confident output caused them to stop verifying against the source. Option B (demographic bias) is a genuine LLM risk category in the abstract but has zero supporting evidence in this audit -- no demographic data was ever collected or referenced. D and E are each anchored to one of the two distinct findings; A, B, and C are each foreclosed by a specific detail in the stem rather than by general implausibility.
questions.topic: LLM failure modes: confabulation and automation bias in a clinical documentation system
questions.objective: Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems

options.label: A
options.text: Prompt injection: the recordings contain adversarial or attacker-crafted phrasing that manipulates the model into inserting an attacker-chosen dosage into the drafted summary.
options.explanation: Incorrect. QA explicitly checked both the recordings and the prior chart for embedded or adversarial phrasing and found none in either input, so there is no evidence any instruction-injection mechanism produced the fabricated numbers.

options.label: B
options.text: Demographic bias: the model produces systematically different, less accurate dosages for specific patient subgroups in this hospital network.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The audit presents no demographic breakdown of the 22 or 15 cases at all; bias against patient subgroups is a real LLM risk in general, but nothing in this audit's evidence points to it here.

options.label: C
options.text: Training-data drift: the model is still drawing on a formulary version that predates a recent dosage-guideline update, so the drafted numbers reflect stale but once-genuine reference values.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The stem states the invented dosages matched no current or previously superseded formulary value for the drug at all -- ruling out a stale-but-real value and pointing instead to outright fabrication.

options.label: D
options.text: Confabulation: the model fabricates a plausible-looking dosage not grounded in the transcript, chart, or any real reference, and fluent phrasing hides the error.
options.explanation: Correct. This is exactly finding #1: a numeric value with no source anywhere (transcript, chart, or any formulary version), reproduced consistently, and delivered in fluent, confidence-inspiring text -- the textbook signature of confabulation.

options.label: E
options.text: Automation bias: reviewers stop verifying drafts against the recording because fluent, confident output has repeatedly seemed reliable, letting errors slip through unnoticed.
options.explanation: Correct. This is finding #2: nurses' own survey admissions describe abandoning word-for-word verification specifically because the AI's fluent, confident tone had built unwarranted trust -- the defining mechanism of automation bias/over-reliance.

questions.text: A fintech company's agent drafts wire-transfer instructions from natural-language requests and submits them to a human approver in a review queue before execution. Audit logs from the past quarter show that in 14% of approved transfers, the analyst clicked "Approve" within 2 seconds of the transfer appearing in the queue — too fast to have read the payee, amount, or account fields. The security team wants to redesign the review checkpoint so approvals reflect genuine scrutiny rather than habitual clicking. Which TWO changes would most strengthen the human-in-the-loop control? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: Correct: A and B. A attacks the observed failure mode directly — it makes the approver actually perceive the changed fields and structurally prevents a sub-second click, a deterministic UI-level guarantee rather than reliance on attentiveness. B concentrates the strongest control (a second, independent approver) on the transfers where a rubber-stamped approval would do the most damage, using a fixed, auditable risk criterion (new payee, amount above historical median). C is a strawman for reason 1 (prompt-when-you-need-a-guarantee): it asks the model to write a risk summary and hopes the analyst reads it, which is exactly the probabilistic reliance that produced the 2-second approvals. D solves an adjacent problem (reason 2): auto-approving low-value transfers reduces reviewer volume but leaves the one-click approval pattern untouched for everything that still reaches a human. E substitutes a relative, batch-dependent threshold for a fixed one (reason 9): a large transfer on a quiet day can still slip through unflagged, reintroducing the inconsistency B's absolute threshold avoids.
questions.topic: Human-in-the-loop validation design for agentic approval workflows
questions.objective: Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies

options.label: A
options.text: Require the approver to open and view the specific changed fields, payee, amount, and account, and disable the Approve button until each field has been on screen for a minimum dwell time.
options.explanation: Correct. Targets the exact observed pattern (2-second approvals) with a deterministic control on the review UI itself, not on the analyst's judgment or attention span.

options.label: B
options.text: Route any transfer with a new payee or an amount above the historical median to a second, independent approver so no single click can authorize the highest-risk transfer.
options.explanation: Correct. Places a structural second check exactly where risk concentrates, using a fixed and auditable criterion, so one rushed click can't clear the transfers that matter most.

options.label: C
options.text: Update the agent's system prompt to draft a short risk summary flagging unusual payees or amounts and ask the analyst to confirm reading it before approving, trusting the summary to catch anything risky.
options.explanation: Wrong. This still depends on the model writing an accurate flag and the analyst choosing to read it before clicking through — the same probabilistic reliance that produced the rubber-stamping in the first place.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a risk-scoring model that automatically approves transfers under $5,000 to an established payee, so analysts spend their attention on the transfers most likely to need judgment.
options.explanation: Wrong. This is a reasonable workload-reduction step, but it addresses transfer volume, not review quality — the transfers that still reach a human are governed by the same unreliable one-click approval the logs describe.

options.label: E
options.text: Flag a transfer for extra scrutiny only when its amount falls in the top 10 percent of that day's batch, so unusually large requests stand out against the day's typical volume.
options.explanation: Wrong. A batch-relative threshold means a large transfer on a light day can go unflagged while a modest one on a heavy day gets flagged — it reintroduces inconsistency instead of the fixed, absolute criterion the scenario calls for.

questions.text:
Match each of the five scenarios below to the single option that best classifies its compliance gap. Options in the shared set may apply to more than one scenario, and some options may not be used at all.

Option set:
A. HIPAA — protected health information handled without a required safeguard
B. GDPR — EU personal data processed in violation of a data-subject right or transfer protection
C. FedRAMP — a cloud product offered to federal agencies without required security review
D. Internal governance gap only — no external regulatory mandate is implicated

1. A telehealth startup receives patient visit transcripts from a hospital partner and uses Claude to draft clinical summaries from them. The startup never signed the formal agreement legally required before a business handles records on behalf of a covered healthcare provider, and its support engineers can read patient names and diagnoses in plaintext debug logs.

2. A Paris-based retailer's Claude-powered support chatbot answers questions from customers across the EU, using each customer's order history for context. A customer in Berlin emails asking the company to erase all personal data tied to their account. Ninety days later, engineering still has no way to purge that customer's records from the system that stores chat context, and no one has responded to the request.

3. A vendor builds a Claude-powered analytics dashboard and sells subscriptions to it as a single hosted product open to any interested federal civilian agency. Three separate agencies have already signed on as customers, yet no agency's security office has ever reviewed the vendor's hosting environment, and the vendor's marketing site advertises the product as "available government-wide."

4. An internal platform team builds a Claude-powered assistant that only reads and summarizes the company's own internal engineering wiki for employees, with no customer, patient, or government data involved anywhere in the pipeline. Before rolling it out company-wide, the team skips the sign-off that company policy requires from the internal architecture review board.

5. A German health-and-fitness app sends users' workout chat transcripts, which include names and home addresses entered during onboarding, to a Claude deployment hosted in a US data center. The company relies solely on the cloud vendor's standard commercial contract terms, without executing any of the extra legal mechanisms required before moving EU residents' personal data to a country outside the EU.
questions.explanation:
Row 1 -> HIPAA: the startup is handling records on behalf of a covered healthcare provider without the formal agreement HIPAA specifically requires in that relationship (a business-associate arrangement), and the plaintext logging of patient names/diagnoses compounds the safeguard failure. This is a legally mandated agreement, not a discretionary internal step, so it cannot be waved off as Option D.

Row 2 -> GDPR: an EU resident invoked their right to erasure and the company let 90 days pass with no mechanism to fulfill it. GDPR gives data subjects an enforceable right with a statutory response window, independent of whatever internal process the company happens to have — so this is a regulatory failure, not merely an unbuilt internal feature.

Row 3 -> FedRAMP: the decisive detail is that this is one hosted product marketed and sold for reuse across multiple federal civilian agencies (three already subscribed), which is precisely the scenario FedRAMP authorization exists to cover — distinct from a single agency running its own internal ATO process (which would instead be a FISMA/NIST RMF matter, not tested here).

Row 4 -> Internal governance gap: the scenario explicitly rules out customer, patient, and government data, leaving only a missed internal architecture-board sign-off — a process failure with no external regulatory hook to attach to.

Row 5 -> GDPR: this is a second, distinct GDPR failure from Row 2. Here EU residents' personal data is moved outside the EU with only a standard commercial contract and none of the legally required transfer mechanisms (e.g., Standard Contractual Clauses or an adequacy finding) in place — an Article 44-49 international-transfer violation, separate from Row 2's right-to-erasure violation. It is not read as HIPAA despite involving health-adjacent data, because HIPAA only reaches US covered entities/business associates, and no such party appears here — the actors are an EU company and EU residents.
