questions.text: During the discovery workshop for a claims-processing assistant, the operations director states the project's only success metric should be "match the current turnaround time." Pulling the legacy system's logs, the architect finds that 12% of closed claims are reopened within 48 hours because supporting documents were missing at closeout — a figure no stakeholder in the room has mentioned. Which action is the most effective next step in requirement gathering?
questions.explanation: D is correct: the architect found a latent requirement (12% reopen rate) in production data that no stakeholder had articulated. Structured discovery means taking that signal back to the stakeholders (including the claims processors who actually see the missing-document cases) to confirm and name it as an explicit requirement before anything is finalized. A takes the operations director's stated requirement as complete and skips validation against the data. B skips ahead to designing a fix before the requirement itself has been agreed and documented. C absorbs the new information into the existing metric via a proportional adjustment rather than surfacing it as its own tracked requirement, which buries the root issue instead of naming it.
questions.topic: Structured discovery and requirement gathering
questions.objective: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering

options.label: A
options.text: Record the operations director's stated turnaround-time target as the sole success metric and move into solution design.
options.explanation: Wrong: it takes the loudest stated requirement at face value and skips validating it against operational data the architect already has in hand, so the reopen-rate driver never gets captured before design starts.

options.label: B
options.text: Convene the documentation team to scope an automated completeness check for supporting documents before setting targets.
options.explanation: Wrong: this jumps straight to a solution (a completeness check) for a requirement that hasn't been named or agreed yet — discovery isn't finished, so committing to a fix is premature.

options.label: C
options.text: Pad the turnaround-time target by 12% to cover reopened claims, then finalize the requirements document.
options.explanation: Wrong: it folds the reopen problem into the existing metric proportionally instead of surfacing it as its own requirement, so the underlying cause stays invisible to stakeholders and untracked going forward.

options.label: D
options.text: Reconvene stakeholders, including claims processors, to name reopen rate as its own requirement.
options.explanation: Correct: the log data surfaced a real success criterion nobody stated; bringing the right stakeholders back in to validate and formally capture it is the structured discovery step before any target or design decision is locked in.

questions.text: Six weeks after launch, the support desk is logging roughly 40 tickets a week from customers asking why refund requests over $500 take 8-12 seconds longer to confirm than smaller ones. The delay is intentional: refunds above that threshold route through a fraud-verification subagent that cross-checks the transaction against a risk-scoring service before releasing funds. That rationale exists only in the architecture repo's design doc, which support never saw. The VP of Customer Experience has now asked the architect for something she can forward to her support directors so they can handle the escalations consistently going forward. What is the most effective way to communicate this architectural decision?
questions.explanation: A is correct: a one-page brief aimed at the actual audience (support directors) that states the threshold, names the cost (latency) and the benefit (fraud reduction) explicitly, and shows how the trade-off can be revisited is exactly the artifact the VP asked for and the level of detail that audience can act on. B fails because it aims a full technical walkthrough — including vendor risk-scoring internals — at an audience that needs a decision summary, not subagent architecture; it's the right instinct (explain the reasoning) pitched at the wrong altitude. C is a manual band-aid: hand-writing 40+ ticket replies a week doesn't scale and still leaves support directors without a durable reference to hand off internally. D solves an adjacent problem — it manages customer-facing confusion at checkout — but the VP's request was for internal stakeholder communication to her directors, not customer copy, so it never actually answers what was asked.
questions.topic: Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Management — communicating architectural trade-offs
questions.objective: Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs

options.label: A
options.text: Send support directors a one-page brief: the $500 threshold, the added latency, the fraud-reduction benefit, and how to adjust the threshold.
options.explanation: Correct. It targets the actual requester (support directors), states the trade-off in plain terms, and gives them a durable, actionable reference for handling future escalations.

options.label: B
options.text: Schedule a session walking each support director through the fraud-verification subagent's internals, including the vendor risk-scoring model it calls.
options.explanation: Wrong altitude: support directors need the decision and its rationale, not a walkthrough of subagent internals and a third-party scoring model; it buries the trade-off the VP actually asked for.

options.label: C
options.text: Have engineering draft individual technical replies to each of the 40 weekly tickets explaining the subagent's routing logic for that refund.
options.explanation: A manual, per-ticket band-aid that doesn't scale past this week's volume and still leaves support directors without anything reusable to brief their teams with.

options.label: D
options.text: Add an in-app banner during checkout noting refunds over $500 undergo extra review, so customers stop opening support tickets about the delay.
options.explanation: Solves an adjacent problem: it may reduce customer confusion at checkout, but it does nothing for the VP's actual request — a document her support directors can use internally.

questions.text: Production dashboards show that a Claude-based support-ticket triage agent missed its 2-minute first-response SLA on 18% of tickets over the past three weeks. The support operations director did not learn of this from the architecture team's reporting, but from a customer escalation email, and is now questioning whether the SLA figures in the quarterly business review can be trusted at all. Which action would most effectively realign stakeholder expectations and prevent this kind of gap from recurring?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B: establishing a recurring stakeholder review built around the live SLA dashboard and pre-agreed escalation thresholds is the only option that creates an ongoing feedback loop between the architecture team and the stakeholder, which is exactly what failed here. A proposes a reasonable SLA renegotiation but still reports it only at the next quarterly cadence, leaving the visibility gap open. C fixes the technical root cause but repeats the same reporting pattern that caused the director to lose trust — information reaches the stakeholder only after the fact. D is a genuinely useful engineering control, but it improves internal alerting, not stakeholder-facing communication, so it solves an adjacent problem rather than the expectation-alignment failure described.
questions.topic: Stakeholder feedback loops and SLA expectation alignment
questions.objective: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)

options.label: A
options.text: Adjust the published SLA target from 2 to 3 minutes based on recent performance data, and present the revised figure on the dashboard at the next quarterly business review.
options.explanation: Renegotiating an SLA to match observed performance is a legitimate move, but doing it as a one-off correction posted to the dashboard only at the next quarterly review still leaves the director dependent on customer escalations in the meantime — it resets the number without building the cadence that would catch the next deviation early.

options.label: B
options.text: Establish a recurring biweekly checkpoint with the director that surfaces real-time performance metrics and pre-agreed thresholds, flagging deviations before customers are affected.
options.explanation: This directly closes the feedback loop: it gives the director recurring, first-hand visibility into real performance against the agreed target and a pre-negotiated trigger for when to escalate, so trust is rebuilt through transparency rather than after-the-fact explanation.

options.label: C
options.text: Have engineering diagnose and resolve the latency regression internally, and report the outcome and escalation history at the next regularly scheduled stakeholder meeting along with quarterly updates.
options.explanation: Fixing the regression is necessary but not sufficient here — folding it, along with a look back at escalation history, into the next routine update repeats the exact pattern that broke trust: the stakeholder finds out about performance issues only after the fact, with no interim visibility or forward-looking escalation path.

options.label: D
options.text: Configure an automated Slack alert that pages the on-call engineer whenever the ticket-triage agent's P95 response latency exceeds the 2-minute SLA threshold.
options.explanation: This is a sound operational safeguard, but it routes information to engineering, not to the stakeholder whose trust was damaged — it solves the internal monitoring gap, not the stakeholder communication and expectation-alignment gap the scenario is actually about.

questions.text: A platform architecture team publishes a design doc for a four-squad multi-agent research pipeline. The doc states that agents "must hand off partial findings to the next agent in a consistent, mutually agreed-upon format," but never defines the format itself. At a week-8 integration test ahead of a mandatory Q3 external security audit, engineers find three of the four squads implemented incompatible handoff schemas (JSON, YAML, and a custom delimited string), causing 42% of cross-squad handoffs to fail undetected. The audit charter requires every agent-to-agent interface to have a versioned, written specification that exists independently of any single implementation, submitted two weeks before integration testing resumes. Which action is most effective for closing this gap before the audit?
questions.explanation: The audit charter's hard requirement -- a versioned, written specification that exists independently of any implementation, due in two weeks -- is what forces C and eliminates the rest. A (recurring review meeting) is a process with no resulting artifact for auditors. B (a reminder line) repeats the same vague language that already caused three squads to diverge, so it isn't a specification at all. D (a shared library) is real engineering effort but is itself an implementation, not the independent written spec the charter demands, and its "next quarter" timeline blows the two-week deadline regardless. Only C -- rewriting the doc's clause into a concrete, versioned schema and enforcing it in CI -- produces the exact artifact the audit requires while directly fixing the root cause of the 42% handoff failures.
questions.topic: stakeholder_lifecycle
questions.objective: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance

options.label: A
options.text: Start a recurring bi-weekly cross-squad review meeting to catch format drift before each squad merges its handoff code.
options.explanation: Wrong: a standing review meeting is a process, not a written artifact. It produces no versioned specification for auditors to inspect, and it's forward-looking review rather than a fix for the three schemas that have already diverged.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a line to the doc reminding squads to use a single, consistent handoff format before their next release.
options.explanation: Wrong: this repeats the exact vague instruction that already produced three incompatible schemas. It still leaves the format undefined, so it satisfies neither the audit's requirement for a concrete spec nor the root cause of the divergence.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace the vague clause with a versioned schema: exact fields, types, header; gate CI on it.
options.explanation: Correct: this turns the ambiguous instruction into the normative, versioned written specification the audit charter demands, independent of any squad's implementation, and CI gating catches nonconforming messages before they cause undetected failures -- deliverable well inside the two-week window.

options.label: D
options.text: Commission a shared serialization library for all squads to import, tracked as next quarter's follow-up epic.
options.explanation: Wrong: a shared library is an implementation, not the independent written specification the audit charter requires -- code alone doesn't give auditors a document to review, and even setting that aside, 'next quarter' misses the two-week submission deadline entirely.

questions.text:
Ten weeks after a Claude-powered support agent went live, the client's dashboard shows the escalation rate climbing from 4% to 19% over three consecutive weeks, with almost every escalated ticket referencing a new subscription tier the client launched five weeks ago. Engineering confirms the agent's knowledge base was never updated to describe the new tier's pricing and cancellation terms. The statement of work states that any change to the agent's knowledge base or routing logic must pass through a change-request process, including a fixed regression-test suite, before it can reach production, and the client's VP has asked engineering to close the gap by the end of the week.

Which approach is most effective given the SOW's change-control requirement?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D. The stem pins down a hard constraint: the SOW mandates a change-request process with a regression-test suite for any knowledge-base or routing change before production deployment. A is disqualified because it explicitly bypasses that required gate under executive pressure. B is disqualified because it escalates a content gap into a full discovery restart, which is disproportionate and ignores the lighter path the SOW already provides. C is disqualified because it treats a missing-information problem as an instruction-following problem, leaving the actual knowledge-base gap unaddressed and never engaging the CR process at all. D is the only option that correctly frames the event as a normal iteration-phase content update and satisfies the stated change-control requirement, making it the one answer forced by the scenario's explicit constraint rather than by unstated preference.
questions.topic: stakeholder_lifecycle
questions.objective: Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)

options.label: A
options.text: Add the missing subscription-tier content directly to the production knowledge base today, skipping the change-request queue this one time since the VP has asked for a resolution within the week.
options.explanation: Wrong: the SOW explicitly requires every knowledge-base change to pass the change-request process and regression suite before reaching production. Executive urgency doesn't waive a contractual gate, and an unvalidated direct patch risks introducing new regressions into a system already under scrutiny.

options.label: B
options.text: Reopen the discovery phase to reassess the agent's overall scope and requirements, treating the new subscription tier as evidence that the original design no longer matches the client's evolving product line.
options.explanation: Wrong: this is a missing content item, not a scope or requirements failure. Restarting discovery is disproportionate, ignores the SOW's lighter-weight change-request path built for exactly this kind of update, and would blow past the VP's timeline.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a system-prompt instruction telling the agent to double-check subscription-tier details before answering and to hedge when uncertain, so the existing knowledge base gap causes fewer confidently wrong answers.
options.explanation: Wrong: the gap is missing factual content, not an instruction-following problem, so a prompt tweak only makes the agent hedge around an absence of information rather than fixing it. It also doesn't touch the knowledge base at all, leaving the SOW's change-request path unused.

options.label: D
options.text: Treat this as a scoped iteration: update the knowledge base with the new tier's pricing and cancellation terms, then route the change through the required change-request process and regression-test suite before it reaches production.
options.explanation: Correct: this identifies the escalation spike as a normal iteration-phase update (new content triggered by a product change, not a design flaw), and it satisfies the SOW's explicit change-control requirement instead of bypassing or over-scoping it, resolving the issue on a timeline the CR process can support.

questions.text: Three weeks into discovery for a claims-processing assistant, workshop notes show the fraud team wants a strict escalation threshold while the operations team wants a faster average resolution time, and the current requirements draft rolls both asks into a single, unowned "accuracy" metric. Which next step is most effective for moving requirement gathering forward?
questions.explanation: A is correct: separating elicitation by stakeholder group before reconciling is the core structured-discovery technique for surfacing and resolving divergent requirements, and it is the shortest option. B defers to sponsor fiat instead of elicitation (manual band-aid). C reaches for automated tooling to solve what a facilitated session already handles (over-engineering). D aligns on wording in a joint session, which fixes the adjacent problem of terminology rather than capturing each team's distinct underlying requirement.
questions.topic: Structured discovery: reconciling conflicting stakeholder requirements
questions.objective: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering

options.label: A
options.text: Interview the fraud and operations teams separately, then reconcile their distinct success metrics into one shared requirements matrix.
options.explanation: Correct. Structured discovery calls for eliciting each stakeholder group's needs independently so divergent, even conflicting, priorities surface in their own terms rather than being averaged away or lost to groupthink. Reconciling the two into a shared, owned matrix turns the vague "accuracy" placeholder into traceable, distinct requirements the design can actually satisfy.

options.label: B
options.text: Escalate the conflict to the project sponsor and adopt whichever single accuracy figure the sponsor assigns, then keep drafting requirements around that number.
options.explanation: Wrong. This is a manual band-aid: a sponsor-issued number resolves the friction on paper but was never elicited from the teams who own the underlying needs, so the fraud and operations requirements stay conflated and untraceable.

options.label: C
options.text: Stand up an automated transcript-analysis tool that flags conflicting terminology across team workshops before the next requirements draft is written.
options.explanation: Wrong. This is premature complexity for a problem a facilitated conversation already solves; building tooling to detect the conflict is a heavier lift than simply talking to each team separately, and it still doesn't produce reconciled requirements on its own.

options.label: D
options.text: Convene a joint session with both teams to agree on one wording for the accuracy metric, then continue the existing discovery workshops as planned.
options.explanation: Wrong. This solves an adjacent problem: aligning on shared vocabulary papers over the disagreement without capturing that fraud and operations actually want different, measurable outcomes, so the underlying requirement conflict resurfaces later in design.

questions.text: Production telemetry for a support-ticket triage system shows that replacing a single Claude agent with a three-agent orchestrator (router, specialist, verifier) cut mis-routed tickets from 18% to 4%, but raised median response latency from 1.2s to 4.9s and monthly token spend from $8K to $31K. The VP of Customer Ops, who approved the original single-agent budget, asks the architecture team to justify the cost increase before the next board review. Which TWO actions are most effective for communicating this architectural trade-off to the VP? (Select 2.)
questions.explanation: A and C are correct. A quantifies the trade-off in the VP's own cost-per-error terms so she can see the net dollar impact of the decision she's being asked to defend. C turns the open-ended cost increase into a bounded, reversible commitment with a concrete rollback trigger, giving her a governance mechanism to approve rather than an indefinite spend. B (cost-attribution dashboard) is a sensible but adjacent investment in future monitoring, not today's justification. D (technical walkthrough of handoff logic and prompt templates) is the wrong altitude of detail for a budget conversation with a VP. E normalizes the spend against an unrelated marketing overrun instead of presenting the actual, absolute trade-off the VP asked about.
questions.topic: Communicating architectural trade-offs to non-technical stakeholders
questions.objective: Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs

options.label: A
options.text: Present a comparison brief that ties the accuracy improvement and the added monthly spend to the support SLA's cost-per-error metric the VP already tracks, showing the net dollar impact of each option.
options.explanation: Correct. It reframes the architecture decision in the business metric the VP already owns and quantifies both sides in dollars, which is what lets her weigh the trade-off rather than just rubber-stamp it.

options.label: B
options.text: Build a per-agent token-attribution dashboard with automated anomaly alerts and a weekly cost-variance report so the VP can monitor spend trends across the router, specialist, and verifier agents going forward.
options.explanation: Wrong. A reasonable future cost-observability investment, but it addresses ongoing spend monitoring, not the immediate need to justify this specific cost increase before the board review.

options.label: C
options.text: Set a 30-day rollback checkpoint: revert to the original, simpler architecture if spend passes $35K without further gains in accuracy, so the VP is approving a bounded trial.
options.explanation: Correct. It converts an open-ended cost increase into a bounded, monitored commitment with a concrete reversal trigger, giving the VP a decision she can approve with a defined downside instead of an indefinite one.

options.label: D
options.text: Schedule a technical walkthrough where the engineering lead demonstrates the router-to-specialist handoff logic and the verifier agent's prompt templates so the VP understands how the architecture works end to end.
options.explanation: Wrong. This communicates how the system works, not why the cost increase is worth it — the wrong level of detail for a VP-level budget-approval conversation.

options.label: E
options.text: Note that this quarter's token spend increase is proportionally smaller than last quarter's marketing budget overrun, so the VP should read the added support-desk cost as acceptable by comparison.
options.explanation: Wrong. Normalizing against an unrelated budget line substitutes a relative comparison for the actual accuracy and SLA impact, giving the VP no absolute business case for this specific decision.

questions.text: Three weeks after go-live, the client's ops team tells the steering committee that the P1 latency alerts they raised in Slack two sprints ago never showed up in the roadmap review, and the account sponsor is now asking whether the 99.5% uptime SLA line item still holds after last month's regional failover cut standby capacity by 20%. Which TWO actions would most effectively re-establish a reliable feedback loop and keep SLA expectations aligned going forward?
questions.explanation: Correct: A and D. A closes the loop that broke — ad hoc Slack reports had no committed handling path or shared visibility, so a tracked queue with response-time commitments prevents issues from silently vanishing before the next review. D addresses the SLA itself: the underlying capacity assumption changed (failover cut standby by 20%), so the commitment must be re-baselined and re-confirmed in writing rather than left stale while the sponsor is already questioning it. B (informal all-hands call) and C (manual Slack triage by one person) are human-in-the-loop patches that don't scale and don't create a durable, auditable feedback channel — they treat the symptom of "issues get missed" without fixing why they got missed. E targets an adjacent problem: internal velocity metrics reassure on delivery pace, not on whether raised concerns are tracked or whether the SLA still reflects reality.
questions.topic: Stakeholder feedback loops and SLA expectation alignment
questions.objective: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)

options.label: A
options.text: Route the flagged issues through a shared tracker with committed response SLAs visible to both teams.
options.explanation: Correct — the reported failure mode is that a raised concern had no committed handling path or shared visibility; a tracked queue with response commitments closes exactly that gap.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a monthly all-hands call so stakeholders can raise concerns the biweekly sync format keeps missing.
options.explanation: Incorrect — another meeting is a manual band-aid; it adds a channel but no commitment or tracking, so issues can still surface and then evaporate before the next review.

options.label: C
options.text: Have the account lead personally scan every support Slack thread before each steering call for early warnings.
options.explanation: Incorrect — a human manually triaging every thread doesn't scale past this account and creates a single point of failure instead of a repeatable process.

options.label: D
options.text: Reissue the uptime commitment for the reduced buffer, and get written sign-off from client leadership.
options.explanation: Correct — the reduced standby buffer invalidated the original uptime assumptions, so the commitment must be re-baselined and formally reconfirmed rather than left ambiguous while client leadership is already questioning it.

options.label: E
options.text: Build an internal dashboard of engineering velocity metrics to reassure the sponsor during steering calls.
options.explanation: Incorrect — velocity metrics address confidence in delivery pace, a different concern than whether raised issues are tracked or whether the SLA terms still hold.

questions.text:
Below are five short situations from an architect's day-to-day work documenting systems and guiding delivery teams. For each one, classify which type of documentation or guidance artifact is the best fit. Choices may be used more than once, and some may not apply at all.

Choose from: Architecture Decision Record (ADR) · Operational runbook · Executive/stakeholder briefing · Reference implementation
questions.explanation:
Option set: ADR, Operational runbook, Executive/stakeholder briefing, Reference implementation.

Row 1 (broker vs. direct calls): The team is weighing several candidate approaches against explicit trade-offs (coupling, latency, cost) and needs the reasoning to survive staff turnover a year later. That is exactly what an ADR is for — capturing a choice among alternatives and why it was made, for an engineering audience that will revisit it. → ADR.

Row 2 (caching layer discarded): A new hire questions a design gap; the tech lead points to a prior write-up explaining that caching was evaluated and rejected for a specific technical reason (stale-data risk). This is the same artifact type as row 1 — a record of a decision (here, a decision NOT to adopt something) being consulted later — which is why ADR keys two different rows without the rows resembling each other on the surface. → ADR.

Row 3 (regional failover): The need is a precise, ordered set of commands and checks to execute under time pressure during an incident, where skipping a step causes data loss. That is an operational runbook's defining trait: procedural, time-critical, executable steps for on-call staff — not a rationale document. → Operational runbook.

Row 4 (board review on migration impact): The audience is a non-technical executive who cares about business risk and release timeline, not service topology or trade-off rationale. Translating architecture impact into business terms for a non-engineering audience is a stakeholder briefing, distinct from an ADR (which targets engineers who need the "why") or a runbook (which targets on-call engineers who need the "how"). → Executive/stakeholder briefing.

Row 5 (inconsistent backoff/circuit-breaker code): Multiple teams implement the same resilience pattern differently, causing inconsistent behavior. The fix is a single canonical, working code example teams can copy — a reference implementation — not a written rationale (ADR), a business summary (briefing), or an incident procedure (runbook).

A candidate who assumes a clean one-to-one mapping across the four options would be forced to misclassify either row 1 or row 2, since both correctly land on ADR while the option "reference implementation" appears only once and nothing forces every option to be used.
questions.topic: Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Management — Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
questions.objective: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance

rows.text: The platform team is choosing between routing order events through a message broker versus having services call each other directly. They've weighed coupling, latency, and operational cost across three candidate approaches and picked one, expecting the reasoning to matter again when the team rotates in a year.

Six months after launch, a new hire asks why the checkout service doesn't use a shared cache despite the obvious performance win. The tech lead pulls up a short write-up from the original design review explaining that caching was tested and discarded because of stale-data risk in this domain.

During a regional outage, the on-call engineer needs the exact sequence of commands and health checks to redirect traffic and promote the standby database, since hesitating or missing a step risks data loss.

Ahead of a board review, a product VP wants to know whether the multi-year migration will affect this quarter's release commitments and what the business risk looks like, without needing to understand the underlying service topology.

Three different teams have each implemented the retry-with-backoff-and-circuit-breaker pattern slightly differently when calling a flaky downstream dependency, causing inconsistent behavior during partial outages. The architecture group wants one canonical, working example that teams can copy.

questions.text: Platform engineering rolled out Claude Code to 40 backend engineers three weeks ago. Support tickets since then show that 15 engineers keep getting stopped by the same permission prompt for `npm test` and `git status` on every session, because each engineer's local settings only reflect whatever they personally approved earlier — there is no shared baseline. The team lead wants any engineer who clones the repo, including new hires next sprint, to inherit the same approved commands and hooks with no manual setup step. Which approach is most likely to close this gap?
questions.explanation: B is correct: Claude Code reads a project-level .claude/settings.json that can be committed to version control, so permissions and hooks defined there are inherited automatically by every clone — exactly the "no manual setup step" requirement. A fails because CLAUDE.md is a natural-language instruction file, not a permissions mechanism; asking Claude to infer approval from repeated prompts relies on probabilistic behavior for something that needs a deterministic guarantee. C targets the wrong scope: ~/.claude/settings.json is per-machine/user-level, so "copy a template then adjust locally" is a manual step repeated per engineer and drifts the moment someone customizes it, not a project-wide baseline. D over-engineers the problem by building a custom allowlist-checking wrapper around the CLI when the built-in settings file already provides this exact capability.
questions.topic: Configuring Claude Code environments for teams (shared permissions/settings)
questions.objective: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)

options.label: A
options.text: Add a CLAUDE.md instruction telling engineers to keep approving the flagged npm test and git status prompts until Claude infers the pattern.
options.explanation: Wrong: CLAUDE.md carries natural-language guidance, not enforceable permission state, so this relies on probabilistic inference rather than the deterministic settings mechanism that already exists.

options.label: B
options.text: Commit a project-level .claude/settings.json with the flagged commands and hooks pre-approved, so every checkout starts from the same baseline automatically.
options.explanation: Correct: a committed project-level settings.json is version-controlled and automatically picked up on clone, giving every engineer the identical baseline with zero manual setup.

options.label: C
options.text: Have each engineer copy a shared template covering the npm test and git status approvals into their personal ~/.claude/settings.json, then adjust permissions locally.
options.explanation: Wrong scope: user-level settings live per machine, so this still requires a manual copy step per engineer and permits drift the moment anyone edits their local file, defeating the shared-baseline goal.

options.label: D
options.text: Wrap the claude CLI in a shell script that checks every command against an internal allowlist file before forwarding it into the Claude Code session.
options.explanation: Over-engineered: it reinvents a custom permission layer as new infrastructure to maintain when the built-in project settings.json already provides shareable, version-controlled permission enforcement.

questions.text: Telemetry from a 40-engineer rollout of Claude Code shows the same roughly 200-word service-scaffolding prompt has been pasted into the CLI 340 times over the past two weeks, with small wording drift between engineers. A follow-up audit finds the generated service is missing its test directory in about 18% of those runs. Which change is most likely to eliminate the inconsistency?
questions.explanation: C wins because the root cause is invocation drift: engineers are freehand-retyping/pasting a long prompt, so the fix is to make invocation deterministic via a project slash command that encodes the exact prompt and checklist (the documented mechanism for exactly this). A is a prompt-strength fix layered on CLAUDE.md that doesn't touch how the prompt gets invoked, so drift and probabilistic compliance both remain. B reaches for a Skill, but Skills are model-invoked — Claude applies them when it judges them relevant — so invocation stays probabilistic; the slash command is the explicit, user-invoked counterpart that runs the identical template deterministically. D solves an adjacent problem with unneeded complexity — subagent isolation addresses context pollution, not inconsistent invocation, and adds a heavier interaction model than the task needs.
questions.topic: Standardizing repeated AI-assisted workflows with slash commands
questions.objective: Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling

options.label: A
options.text: Add a scaffolding-standards paragraph to the root CLAUDE.md directing Claude to always generate a matching test directory for the new service.
options.explanation: This only strengthens an instruction Claude probabilistically follows; it doesn't stop engineers from retyping and varying the underlying prompt, so the drift that causes the missing directories keeps happening even with the added guidance.

options.label: B
options.text: Package the scaffolding procedure as a project Skill so Claude discovers and applies the team standard whenever it judges a scaffolding task is underway.
options.explanation: A Skill is model-invoked: Claude decides when it applies, so invocation stays probabilistic — the failure here is inconsistent invocation, and only an explicit user-invoked command guarantees the identical template runs every time.

options.label: C
options.text: Author a project slash command, .claude/commands/scaffold-service.md, encoding the prompt and a required-files checklist so engineers run /scaffold-service instead of retyping it.
options.explanation: A project slash command is the documented mechanism for turning a repeated free-form prompt into one deterministic, versioned invocation, which directly removes the copy-paste wording drift causing the missing test directories.

options.label: D
options.text: Package the scaffolding steps as a dedicated subagent with its own isolated context window, launched explicitly by an engineer for each new service.
options.explanation: A subagent's isolated context is meant for offloading exploration that would otherwise pollute the main conversation; it adds architectural overhead here without fixing the actual problem, which is that engineers invoke the task inconsistently.

questions.text: An internal on-call tool wraps the Claude Code SDK to triage incident tickets: it reads the last 500 lines of application logs, has Claude classify a likely root cause, and posts that classification as a ticket comment. Ops dashboards show that 12% of triage runs post the identical comment "No root cause identified from available logs." While investigating a recent P1, an engineer discovered that one such run had actually crashed midway through parsing: a new structured-logging format had shipped the prior week, and the parser raised a KeyError when it hit older-format log records still mixed in during rollout. The triage script's top-level exception handler catches every exception and falls back to posting that same generic negative message, so the crash was indistinguishable from a genuine "nothing found" result — the on-call engineer only caught it by rerunning the tool manually with verbose output. The incident runbook mandates that any tool crash during triage must be visibly distinguishable in the ticket from a genuine negative finding, since conflating the two already caused one missed escalation. Which change most effectively brings the tool into compliance with that runbook requirement going forward?
questions.explanation: The stem pins down a hard runbook requirement -- any tool crash during triage must be visibly distinguishable from a genuine "no root cause found" result -- and grounds it in a concrete failure (12% of runs post an identical fallback comment; one such run was actually a KeyError crash from a schema rollout, caught only by manual rerun). A (prompting the model to "try harder") targets the wrong stage entirely, since the failure happened before Claude was ever called. B (blind retry) reruns a deterministic failure and still ends at the same generic message, so the ambiguity the runbook forbids persists. C (schema-aware routing) is a real and useful fix for this one log format, but it doesn't touch the exception handler that swallows failures generally, so the runbook's requirement -- covering any crash, not just this one -- remains unmet. D is the only option that changes the actual failure-surfacing mechanism: narrow the catch to expected exceptions and give any other exception its own distinctly labeled comment, so crashes can never again be mistaken for a genuine negative finding.
questions.topic: developer_productivity: surfacing tool crashes vs. genuine negative results in Claude-powered on-call triage
questions.objective: Support debugging and operational issue resolution

options.label: A
options.text: Add explicit few-shot examples and stronger system-prompt instructions telling the model to keep searching logs harder before concluding no root cause is found, so genuinely findable root causes are not reported as absent.
options.explanation: Wrong problem: the run in question never even reached the model, because the parser raised a KeyError before Claude was invoked. Strengthening prompt instructions only changes Claude's behavior when it runs, so a crash upstream of the model call would still fall into the same generic fallback and remain invisible.

options.label: B
options.text: Wrap the entire triage pipeline in a retry loop that reruns the log-parsing and root-cause analysis up to three times on any exception before falling back to the existing generic no-root-cause message.
options.explanation: The schema mismatch is deterministic, so retrying reproduces the identical KeyError each time and the pipeline still lands on the same generic fallback message. The crash remains indistinguishable from a genuine negative finding, which is precisely what the runbook prohibits.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a log-format detection step at startup that routes each incident log bundle to a dedicated parser chosen from the source's declared schema version, so the new structured-logging format is parsed correctly.
options.explanation: This is a sensible fix for this specific schema mismatch, but it leaves the top-level exception handler untouched. Any other future exception -- a different malformed record, a network hiccup during log fetch -- will still be absorbed into the same generic message, so the runbook's general requirement is still unmet.

options.label: D
options.text: Limit automatic recovery to the handful of parsing failures already anticipated, and for anything else, publish a clearly labeled failure notice naming what broke instead of reusing the wording reserved for a genuine clean result.
options.explanation: Correct: this directly satisfies the runbook. Any crash, present or future, now surfaces as its own clearly labeled failure notice rather than being folded into the same wording used for a genuine negative result, letting on-call engineers tell the two apart without having to rerun the tool manually.

questions.text: A repo audit for the payments-api project finds that 14 of the 22 engineers have hand-copied the same permission allowlist and MCP server entries into their personal ~/.claude/settings.json. A newer engineer's copy was missing a deny rule blocking Bash access outside the repo, and it let a stray cleanup command reach a scratch directory during a live demo. Which TWO changes should the platform team make so every engineer on the project gets the same permissions and MCP tooling automatically, while still being able to layer personal overrides on top?
questions.explanation: A and E together give the platform team both halves of a shared, version-controlled configuration: .claude/settings.json for permission rules and .mcp.json for MCP servers, each loaded automatically for every engineer while settings.local.json still allows personal overrides. B fails because CLAUDE.md is read as instructions, not enforced as a permission control. C solves a broader problem than asked (org-wide lock-in) and removes the override flexibility the team still wants. D is the same manual copy-paste process that already caused the incident, just repeated on a schedule.
questions.topic: Claude Code: shared project settings, .mcp.json, and enterprise managed policy for teams
questions.objective: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)

options.label: A
options.text: Commit a project-level `.claude/settings.json` with the shared allow/deny rules, and route individual tweaks through a gitignored `.claude/settings.local.json`.
options.explanation: Correct. A committed project-level settings.json is the documented mechanism for a team to share permission rules through source control, and settings.local.json is the paired, gitignored layer meant for individual overrides — exactly the split the incident is missing.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the permission allowlist as a section in the repo's CLAUDE.md so Claude follows the rules at the start of each session.
options.explanation: Wrong. CLAUDE.md is prompt context the model reads and tries to follow, not an enforced permission gate — it relies on probabilistic compliance for a control that needs to be deterministic, which is exactly the kind of gap that let the stray command through.

options.label: C
options.text: Configure an enterprise managed policy file that locks the same rules and MCP servers for every repo across the whole organization.
options.explanation: Wrong. This is the right mechanism at the wrong scope: an org-wide managed policy would standardize every project, not just payments-api, and it overrides rather than layers with local settings — heavier than the single-team problem calls for.

options.label: D
options.text: Document the exact JSON block for the rules and MCP entries on the team wiki, and have each of the 22 engineers copy it into their own settings file next sprint.
options.explanation: Wrong. This is a manual, human-driven rollout of the same copy-paste process that already produced the drift and the missing deny rule — it doesn't scale and will decay again the next time a rule changes.

options.label: E
options.text: Add a `.mcp.json` file at the project root listing the MCP servers the project relies on, so they load the moment anyone opens the repo.
options.explanation: Correct. Project-scoped MCP servers belong in a committed .mcp.json, so the same server list loads for every engineer without hand-editing personal config — the MCP-side counterpart to the shared settings.json for permissions.
